questions.stem: Defense counsel conceded that the page had been omitted but insisted the omission was {1} rather than {2} — the work of a clerk too tired to notice at two in the morning, not of anyone who had weighed in advance what its absence would accomplish.
questions.explanation: The dash-clause splits the sentence in two: exhaustion maps to {1} and prior weighing of consequences maps to {2}, so the pair must be accident versus forethought. Deliberate is the word for an act whose consequences were weighed beforehand, which is exactly why prosecutors reach for it; impetuous and precipitate would describe acting without thought, the opposite of what counsel is denying.

questions.stem: Officers who expected the temperament of a man famous for cavalry charges to be {1} were startled by the {2} progress of his first campaign: three weeks of surveying ground and questioning farmers before a single order to advance was issued.
questions.explanation: "Startled by" demands that the two blanks oppose each other, and the colon defines the second: weeks of preparation before acting. That is deliberate in its pace sense — unhurried because the thing is being given the time it deserves — while the expectation set up by cavalry charges is impetuousness; circumspect and judicious would remove the surprise entirely.

questions.stem: Where his predecessors had ruled from the bench within minutes of the final argument, Judge Hallam would {1} for weeks over a single evidentiary question, and litigants learned to expect no ruling before the next term.
questions.explanation: The contrast with ruling "within minutes" calls for a verb of prolonged private thought, which deliberate and cogitate both supply. Temporize is the trap: it fits the delay but attributes it to stalling for advantage rather than to thinking, and demur (to object) and expatiate (to speak at length) describe the wrong activity altogether.

questions.stem: Nothing in the memoir is uproarious: its humour is {1}, so flatly delivered and so seldom signalled that half the audience misses the joke, and the reviewers who complained of the book's {2} had merely mistaken deadpan for solemnity.
questions.explanation: Humour that is flat, unsignalled, and easily missed is droll; facetious wit is conspicuously jokey, which is what "seldom signalled" rules out. The second blank must name what a reader who missed the joke would wrongly accuse the book of — excessive gravity, i.e. staidness — whereas levity would mean they had detected the comedy after all.

questions.stem: A famously {1} companion at dinner, Lamb would offer his oddest observations in the flat, faintly puzzled tone of a man reporting the weather, so that his guests often laughed a full sentence late.
questions.explanation: The delayed laughter and the weather-report delivery point to dry, understated, peculiar wit — droll. Sardonic would require mockery or bitterness, which the faintly puzzled tone excludes, and bombastic, garrulous, and effusive all describe an excess of manner incompatible with flatness.

questions.stem: The village regarded his habits — the forty clocks, the purple suit worn daily for thirty years — as {1} rather than alarming, the harmless fixtures of a man everyone had known since boyhood.
questions.explanation: "Rather than alarming" and "harmless" fix the sense as odd but tolerated, which eccentric and quirky both give. Iconoclastic would make the oddity an assault on received belief rather than a private habit, affected would make it a pose rather than genuine, and hidebound and doctrinaire denote rigid conventionality — the reverse of odd.

questions.stem: Though his colleagues filed him away as merely {1} — the cape, the rescued owls, the refusal to keep a telephone — the published work was in fact fiercely {2}, overturning the very assumptions on which three generations of the discipline had been built.
questions.explanation: "Though ... merely ... in fact" sets harmless personal oddity against genuine intellectual assault: the cape and the owls are eccentricity, a tolerated private strangeness, while overturning a discipline's founding assumptions is iconoclasm. Whimsical would keep the work in the same harmless register the concession is meant to exceed, and orthodox contradicts the overturning outright.

questions.stem: The coalition held together only while its founder lived; within a month of his funeral it had grown so {2} that ministers were briefing against one another in the Sunday papers, and correspondents who had once admired its discipline now doubted that any {1} could last out the session.
questions.explanation: Ministers briefing against one another is internal squabbling that threatens to split the group, which is precisely the collective use of fractious; doctrinaire would describe rigid ideology rather than mutual sniping, and stoic reverses the sense. What such squabbling destroys is comity — courteous relations among members — not autonomy or levity.

questions.stem: The ward sister's notes described the patient not as dangerous but merely as {1}: resistant to every routine, aggrieved by the food, and forever ringing the bell for trifles.
questions.explanation: "Not as dangerous but merely" rules out truculent, belligerent, and pugnacious, all of which imply an aggressive threat, while stoic contradicts the complaining. Fractious is exactly the nurse's word for a cranky, resistant charge — a nuisance to manage, described from a position of authority.
